posts.title: Lower back on site
posts.about: Tradie-week opener: five free habits that protect the lower back, with Ben M's words on the last slide.
posts.headline: Lower back on site: five free habits
posts.subline: None of them cost a cent.

slides.h: Lower back on site: five habits that cost nothing
slides.b: Most site back pain builds over weeks, not one bad lift. Swipe for five small habits that add up.

slides.h: 1. Warm up before the first lift
slides.b: Two minutes of hip circles, squats and a walk around the site. Cold backs complain first.
Hold it against your body, bend at the hips and knees, and turn with your feet, not your back.
Kneeling, bending or sitting in the ute. Stand up, stretch tall and reset before you carry on.
Two people, a trolley or a lighter load. It is not slower if it keeps you on the tools next month.

slides.h: 5. Look after the drive home and the night
slides.b: Sit back in the seat, stop on long drives, and get your sleep. Recovery happens off site. See your GP if pain spreads down a leg.
Ben M, electrician and sportsman, Auckland. Real words from a real customer.

posts.caption:
Most lower back pain on site builds slowly. Small habits stop it building.

Five that cost nothing:
1. Warm up for two minutes before the first lift.
2. Keep the load close and turn with your feet.
3. Change position every 30 minutes.
4. Ask for a hand with the heavy stuff.
5. Look after the drive home and your sleep.

If your back pain comes with numbness, weakness, pain down a leg, or any change to your bladder or bowel, see your GP straight away. That is not one to rub and wait on.

For the everyday ache after a long day, a proper massage with a rub helps you wind down. Our Joints and Sports rubs are made with native NZ herbs, 11 to 14 active ingredients in every jar.

Save this for the smoko room.

posts.title: Tennis elbow isn't just tennis
posts.about: Injury first aid post on tennis elbow from repetitive gripping, the second of the week's three tradie injuries.
posts.headline: Tennis elbow isn't just tennis
posts.subline: Drill, paintbrush, phone. Same tendon, same ache.

steps.t: Change your grip, swap hands, take short breaks from the drill or brush.
Gentle wrist and forearm strengthening, little and often, once the sharp pain settles.
Massage a rub into the forearm and outer elbow, morning and night.

posts.caption:
Tennis elbow is pain on the outside of the elbow, and most people who get it have never held a racquet.

It comes from the same small movement repeated: gripping a drill, painting a ceiling, pruning, scrolling a phone. The tendon on the outside of the elbow gets more load than it can recover from.

What helps:
1. Ease the load. Change your grip, swap hands, take breaks.
2. Build it back with gentle forearm strengthening once the sharp pain settles.
3. Massage a rub into the forearm and outer elbow, morning and night.

It can take weeks to settle. If it came from a fall, the elbow is swollen, or your hand is numb or weak, see your GP or a physio.

Our Sports and Joints rubs are made for exactly this kind of ache.

posts.title: Medicines linked to muscle pain
posts.about: Wellness carousel from the blog: common medicines that can cause muscle aches, and why the first step is a GP or pharmacist, not stopping the medicine.
posts.headline: Seven medicines linked to muscle pain
posts.subline: And what to do if you're on one.

slides.h: Seven common medicines linked to muscle pain
slides.b: If you started a new medicine and your muscles started aching, the two might be connected. Swipe, then talk to your GP.
Cholesterol medicines. Aching legs and shoulders are a known side effect for some people. Your GP can review the dose or try another.
A group called fluoroquinolones is linked to tendon and muscle pain. Tell your doctor straight away if a tendon hurts while you're on one.
Longer courses of corticosteroids can weaken muscles, often in the hips and thighs.
{MEDICINES 4 TO 7 FROM BLOG}. The full list, and why each one can cause aches, is on our blog.
Don't stop your medicine on your own. Note when the aches started, then talk to your GP or pharmacist. Often there is an easy fix.
For everyday aches while you sort it out, a gentle massage with a natural rub can help you stay comfortable. Read the full article: link in bio.

posts.caption:
If a new medicine and new muscle aches arrived at the same time, they might be connected.

Some common medicines are linked to muscle pain as a side effect: statins for cholesterol, some antibiotics, longer courses of steroid tablets, and a few others. It doesn't happen to everyone, and it's often easy to sort.

The most important thing: don't stop a prescribed medicine on your own. Write down when the aches started, then talk to your GP or pharmacist. They can check the dose or suggest another option.

For everyday comfort while you sort it out, a gentle massage with a natural rub can help. Please check with your pharmacist that it suits you alongside your medicines.

The full list of seven is on our blog. Link in bio.

shots.shot: Joints Rub jar opened, a hand massaging it into a knee

posts.caption:
Tūpākihi is the herb most people have never heard of, and the one with some of the most interesting lab results.

It's herb ten of our eleven, and it lives in our Joints Rub. In independent lab tests (Trinity Bioactives), Tūpākihi oil reduced COX-2 activity, a pathway linked to inflammation, by 28.4%. That was a test on cells, not people, so we share it as what it is: an encouraging early result.

One important thing: the wild plant is poisonous. Please never pick it, eat the berries or make anything from it at home.

Tūpākihi is traditionally used in rongoā rākau. Our Joints Rub is made for stiffness and the long-term aches that come with it.

posts.title: Sleep is recovery
posts.about: Wellness post: three free sleep habits that matter more than any product, and the small place a rub has in a wind-down.
posts.headline: Sleep is recovery
posts.subline: Three things that beat any product.

steps.t: Get up at the same time daily, weekends too. Your body clock follows.
A cooler room, blackout curtains and the phone out of reach.
Thirty minutes off screens. A slow massage with a rub fits here.

posts.caption:
Your body does most of its repair while you sleep. No product beats a good night.

Three habits that help most:
1. Same wake time every day, weekends too.
2. A cool, dark, quiet room, with the phone out of reach.
3. Thirty minutes of wind-down before bed, off screens.

Where does a rub fit? As part of that wind-down. A slow massage into whatever aches tells your body the day is over.

"I've never slept like this." Tracey, New Zealand.

If pain wakes you most nights, or you're tired no matter how long you sleep, talk to your GP. It's worth getting checked.

steps.t: Rest, ice wrapped in a cloth, compress and raise it for 48 hours.
Cold first, then gentle massage once the swelling settles.
Stop every two hours, walk, stretch, then rub it in.

posts.caption:
Long weekends bring long drives, new tracks and backyard games. Here's what to do in the first 48 hours if something hurts.

Rolled ankle: rest it, ice wrapped in a cloth for 15 to 20 minutes, a firm bandage, and keep it raised.
Bumps and bruises: cold first, then a gentle massage with a rub once the swelling settles.
Stiff after the drive: stop every two hours, walk and stretch.

If you can't put weight on it, the pain is severe, or something looks out of shape, see a doctor or call Healthline on 0800 611 116.

Keep a Relief Rub in the bach or the car. This weekend, shipping is free anywhere in New Zealand: {OFFER DETAILS}.

Harakeke, Horopito, Kūmarahou, Kōwhai, Koromiko, Pūriri, Rātā, Pukatea, Kahikatea, Tūpākihi and Karaeo. Each one is traditionally used in rongoā rākau, and each one grows here in Aotearoa.

On Waitangi Day we're simply grateful: for the land these plants come from, and for the knowledge of the people who understood them first.

Ngā mihi o Te Rā o Waitangi.

slides.h: Eleven herbs, all of them, one post
slides.b: Every native herb we use, which range it's in, and one thing to know. Save this.
Harakeke, NZ flax: Relief and Sports. Horopito, the pepper tree: Relief. Kūmarahou, the gumdiggers' soap: Joints and Sports.
Kōwhai: Sports. Koromiko, the herb every Kiwi grandmother knew: Relief. Pūriri: Sports.
Rātā, the red-flowering tree: Relief. Pukatea, the swamp forest giant: Joints and Sports. Kahikatea, our tallest tree: Relief.
Tūpākihi: Joints. Poisonous in the wild, never pick it. Karaeo, the climbing vine: Joints.

posts.caption:
Eleven native herbs, all of them, in one post. Save this.

Relief: Harakeke, Horopito, Kahikatea, Rātā, Koromiko.
Joints: Tūpākihi, Kūmarahou, Pukatea, Karaeo.
Sports: Harakeke, Kūmarahou, Kōwhai, Pukatea, Pūriri.

Some herbs work in two ranges. None of our jars holds all eleven, because each range is blended for a different job: Relief for everyday aches, Joints for stiffness and mobility, Sports for warm-up and recovery.

Every one of them is traditionally used in rongoā rākau, and we credit that knowledge.

posts.title: A parent's sideline kit
posts.about: Injury first aid for parents heading back to Saturday sport: what to pack and what to do with the common bumps.
posts.headline: A parent's kit for Saturday sport
posts.subline: Back to school, back to the sidelines.

steps.t: Water, snacks, an ice pack, a bandage, plasters and a Relief Rub.
Cold first for 15 minutes, then gentle massage once swelling settles.
Off the field, rest, ice, compress, raise. No play until it's pain-free.

posts.caption:
School's back, which means Saturday sport is back, and so are the knocks.

What to pack in the sideline bag: water, snacks, an ice pack, a bandage, plasters, sunscreen and a Relief Rub.

Knocks and bruises: cold for 15 minutes, then a gentle massage once any swelling settles.
Rolled ankles: off the field, rest, ice, a firm bandage and keep it raised. No more play until it's pain-free.

Head knocks are different. If your child has a knock to the head and seems dazed, sick, sleepy or not themselves, take them off and see a doctor. When in doubt, sit them out.

Our Relief range is suitable for children over five. Save this for Saturday.

posts.title: Trials warm-up for kids
posts.about: Wellness Reel: a 20-second warm-up for netball and rugby trials that looks after ankles and knees.
posts.headline: A 20-second warm-up for trials
posts.subline: Netball and rugby. Ankles and knees first.

shots.shot: Kids jogging onto a school field, morning light
A child doing quick high knees
Side shuffles along a sideline, low and light
Calf raises, slow up and down
Small hops, landing soft with bent knees

posts.caption:
Most trial-day ankle and knee injuries happen in the first ten minutes, before muscles are warm.

A 20-second warm-up kids can do on their own:
High knees.
Side shuffles.
Calf raises.
Small hops, landing soft with knees over toes.

Then a few minutes of easy jogging and passing before the trial starts. Landing soft and keeping the knees in line with the toes is the habit worth teaching early.

If an ankle or knee swells, or your child can't put weight on it, stop and get it checked by a doctor or physio.

Good luck to everyone trialling this week. Save this for the car park.

steps.t: Relief for everyday aches, Joints for stiffness, Sports for warm-up and recovery.
1 to 5 ml, massaged in, up to five times a day.
Relief from five. Joints and Sports from seven. Not in pregnancy.

posts.caption:
Three months of question boxes, comments and one Facebook Live. These came up most.

Which one is right for me? Relief for everyday aches and the family, Joints for stiffness and mobility, Sports for warm-up and recovery.

How much should I use? 1 to 5 ml, massaged in, up to five times a day. It works best after a shower, when your skin is warm. Patch test first.

Is it safe for kids? Relief from age five, Joints and Sports from seven. Not while pregnant or breastfeeding.

Heat or ice? Ice for a fresh injury in the first 48 hours. Gentle warmth for stiff muscles and joints.

{MOST-ASKED QUESTION FROM INSIGHTS}

posts.title: Autumn sport preview
posts.about: The week's promo: what autumn brings for sport and the body, with the range reminder in the last line.
posts.headline: Autumn is coming: what to expect
posts.subline: New seasons, cooler mornings, stiffer joints.
posts.caption:
Autumn changes what hurts. Winter codes start pre-season, mornings get colder, and stiff joints notice it first.

What to expect, and what helps:
Pre-season for netball, rugby, football and hockey. Build up slowly: the 10% rule still applies.
Cooler mornings. Warm up for longer before the walk, the round of golf or the garden.
Stiffer joints. Keep moving little and often, and give them a warm massage at the end of the day.

This autumn we'll be sharing more on joints, winter sport and herb stories from the bush. Follow along so you don't miss it.

For the season ahead, our Relief, Joints and Sports ranges are online and in 200+ stores around Aotearoa. Link in bio.
